To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
sex-related differences in the pharmacokinetic parameters and the pharmacologic effects (including the risk of adverse events) of antiretrovirals are increasingly being reported in women.
sex differences exist in the pharmacologic responses to antiretovirals and these differences may be related to sex differences in drug transporters and drug metabolizing enzymes.

(1) sex differences in the expression and activities of enzymes and transporters involved in drug disposition may contribute to sex differences in drug responses; (2) sex differences in drug disposition are likely to be complex and involve interactions among multiple factors including genetic, physiologic, and environmental factors; and (3) further research is needed to determine the extent to which sex differences in drug transporters and metabolic enzymes contribute to sex differences observed in treatment responses
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of drug metabolizing enzymes, drug transporters and sex in the disposition of antiretrovirals.
the role of sex differences in the disposition of drugs, particularly antiretrovirus, and how this may contribute to sex-related differences in antiviral drug responses.
the identification of the mechanisms that contribute to sex-related differences in drug effects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of drug transporters in antiretrovirus drug disposition and sex differences in the pharmacological effects of antiretovirus drugs are not fully elucidated.
sex differences in the levels of enzymes involved in drug disposition may partly contribute to observed sex differences in treatment responses.

sex-related differences in the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of antiretrovirals may be partly due to differences in the levels of drug transporters, metabolizing enzymes, and their activities between men and women.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

sex differences in the pharmacological effects of antiretovirals are likely to be influenced by the expression and activity of drug transporters (particularly breast cancer resistance protein) and metabolising enzymes (particularly CYP2C9, 2C19 and 3A4).
sex differences in the pharmacokinetics of antiretrovirals may be explained by sex differences in the levels of drug transporters, phase 1, and phase 2 metabolizing enzyme activities.
sex differences in the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of antiretrovirals can be attributed to sex-related differences in the expression and activities of transporters and metabolizers.
The main takeaway from our work is that

women may be more susceptible than men to the adverse effects of certain antiretrovirus drugs, such as protease inhibitors, and that this susceptibility may be related, in part, to differences in the levels of drug transporters in the liver and intestine and in the levels of activity of certain drug-metabolizing enzymes in the liver.

the pharmacologic effects and disposition of antiretrovirals in women may differ from those in men, and this difference is likely to be mediated by sex-related differences in expression and activity of enzymes and drug transport proteins involved in drug disposition.
women may be more sensitive than men to the pharmacologic effects, including adverse effects of antiviral drugs.
